# Materials and Methods

@fig-overview presents an overview of the workflow. Using time-lapse imagery, we (i) produced vegetation classification maps for 2012 and 2021 to quantify 9-year changes in *Sasa* distribution and (ii) characterized the snowmelt pattern and its temporal trend from per-cell snowmelt dates for 2011–2021, expressed as day of year (DOY). We then (iii) fitted two statistical models: a habitat suitability model of environmental potential (Model A) and an establishment model of the observed 2012–2021 establishment (Model B), and (iv) projected establishment to 2030 under explicit snowmelt scenarios using a stochastic cellular automaton based on Model B. All spatial analyses used a common 1 m grid (JGD2011 / UTM zone 53N, EPSG:6690). Throughout, **cell** denotes a unit of this 1 m analysis grid, whereas **pixel** denotes a pixel of the camera images.

![Images from a single fixed camera support two models corresponding to the two modes of *Sasa* expansion and projections of future establishment. Alignment, classification, and georectification of the time-lapse imagery (2011–2021) produce vegetation maps for 2012 and 2021 and the mean snowmelt date of every 1 m cell; terrain variables are derived from a digital elevation model (DEM). Model A (habitat suitability) relates presence in 2021 to the environmental predictors (mean snowmelt date and terrain); suitable but unoccupied area defines the seed-dispersal stratum. Model B (establishment) relates observed 2012→2021 establishment to distance from the 2012 front and the same environmental predictors. A stochastic cellular automaton applies Model B annually from 2022 to 2030, recomputing the distance surface as simulated fronts advance under snowmelt scenarios (s = 0 or −0.71 days/year), and the resulting establishment probabilities by 2030 define the rhizome stratum, communities at risk from front advance.](files/fig01_workflow.png){#fig-overview width=100%}

## Study site {#sec-study-site}

The study slope is located on the western side of Mt. Tateyama (Murodo-daira and the surrounding slopes, 2,350–3,015 m a.s.l.) in the northern Japanese Alps, within Chubu-Sangaku National Park, Toyama Prefecture. This region is among the snowiest alpine environments in the world. Airborne laser surveys conducted at peak snow accumulation showed that mean snow depth on the western slope of Mt. Tateyama increases linearly with elevation, reaching approximately 6–7 m at Murodo-daira, with substantially greater local depths in snowdrifts [@Iida2006JSSI]. The plateau consists of pyroclastic deposits from Tateyama Volcano, and the slopes are dissected by avalanche tracks and hollows that retain snow. Snowmelt progresses from wind-exposed ridges, typically during May–June, to snowbed hollows where snow persists into August, creating steep gradients in growing-season length over horizontal distances of tens of meters.

The vegetation forms a mosaic characteristic of the snowy alpine zone of central Japan, comprising dwarf pine scrub on exposed sites, snowbed communities in late-melting hollows, tall-forb meadows on moist slopes, and deciduous shrubs (rowans, maple, and montane alder) along streams and avalanche tracks. *Sasa* forms dense stands near the lower limit of the alpine zone and occurs as scattered patches on the study slope. Although the area receives intensive tourist use via the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route, visitors remain on the maintained trails, and the observed slope is not directly affected by trampling. Neither vegetation management nor *Sasa* removal occurred on the slope during the study period.

## Image acquisition {#sec-image-acquisition}

Images were captured using a digital time-lapse camera (EOS 5D Mark II, Canon Inc., 21 megapixels) installed by the National Institute for Environmental Studies on the Murodo-sanso mountain lodge (approximately 2,450 m a.s.l.). Since 2010, the camera has photographed the slope hourly from 6:00 to 19:00 between April and November. Details of the camera installation and operation are given in @Okamoto2024RSEC. Vegetation classification used seven frames (single photographs) per year, acquired between late August and mid-October of 2012 and 2021 at intervals of approximately 1–2 weeks, and snowmelt detection used images from April to August of each year during 2011–2021. Data from 2019 are missing because of construction work at the mountain lodge housing the camera. Images from 2010 were excluded because a different lens gave an incompatible field of view. Snowmelt detection followed the workflow of @IdeOguma2013EcolInfom, which is based on Otsu's binarization method [@otsu_binarization]. Detectable snowmelt dates were censored by the imaging season (approximately DOY 120–230), and pixels without valid detections, including sky and permanently occluded terrain, were treated as missing.

## Vegetation classification maps {#sec-classification}

Vegetation classification maps were generated using the three-step pipeline of @Okamoto2024RSEC.

- **Image alignment.** All frames from both years were aligned to a common reference image so that each pixel refers to the same location on the slope in every frame. Alignment was performed by matching local image features between frames using the AKAZE feature detector and estimating the geometric transformation between images while discarding mismatched features (projective transformation fitted with the RANSAC robust-estimation algorithm), implemented in OpenCV. Median residual misalignment between the 2012 and 2021 series was 1–2 pixels, with no systematic offset between years.
- **Vegetation classification.** Each pixel was assigned to one of seven classes: dwarf pine (*Pinus pumila*), dwarf bamboo (*Sasa* spp.), rowans (*Sorbus sambucifolia*, *S. matsumurana*), maple (*Acer tschonoskii*), montane alder (*Alnus viridis* subsp. *maximowiczii*), other vegetation (alpine herbs and dwarf shrubs, such as crowberry and avens), and no vegetation. The classifier was a convolutional recurrent neural network (Conv2D–LSTM on 5×5-pixel patches) that uses temporal changes in leaf color across seasonal image sequences. The training labels comprised 216 hand-drawn polygons delineated mainly on the 2015 imagery and verified against the 2012 and 2021 image sequences. Overall accuracy in 5-fold cross-validation was 0.982 for the 2012 series and 0.975 for the 2021 series (class-specific accuracy, network architecture, and training procedures are provided in the Supporting Information; Table S2). However, cross-validation splits were performed at the pixel level rather than the polygon level, and the same labeled polygons were applied to both years. Therefore, these estimates disproportionately reflect classification performance near the training polygons, whereas accuracy at unseen locations farther from the training data may be lower.
- **Georectification.** Ground control points were automatically extracted from orthorectified aerial photographs and a DEM to estimate camera parameters. Images were then projected onto the 1 m analysis grid using the Python package `alproj` (<https://github.com/0kam/alproj>) [@Okamoto2024RSEC]. The median ground-control-point residuals were approximately two pixels, and the raster maps were completed with a single gap-filling pass using a 3×3 modal filter.

## Quantification of *Sasa* change {#sec-sasa-change}

The 2012 and 2021 vegetation maps were overlaid (Figure S5) and a transition matrix was calculated for all classes. Three measures of change were distinguished: **gross expansion**, the area transitioning from non-*Sasa* to *Sasa*; **gross loss**, the area transitioning from *Sasa* to non-*Sasa*; and **net change**, the difference between the two. Areas were reported as the sum of the geodesic areas of 1 m cells measured on the Earth's ellipsoid. These are nearly identical to the nominal areas calculated as cell count × 1 m² (difference <0.1%); figure legends and model sample sizes refer to cell counts. Because *Sasa* can persist beneath shrub canopies, apparent losses may reflect canopy cover or shifts in the classification of mixed *Sasa*–shrub pixels rather than true decline. The destination classes of losses are reported in the Results section, and this ambiguity is addressed in the Discussion section. To test whether apparent losses to dwarf pine were concentrated along vegetation boundaries, Euclidean distances from every *Sasa*→dwarf pine cell to the nearest 2012 dwarf pine cell were calculated and grouped into classes (≤1.5, 1.5–3, 3–5, and >5 m). All 2012 *Sasa* cells were used as the reference distribution; transition cells more than 5 m from 2012 dwarf pine were grouped into clusters by 8-neighbor connectivity and inspected individually (Table S4, Figure S6). To empirically assess the nature of the transitions, a blind interpretation of the paired images was conducted. A total of 129 samples comprised 79 loss cells allocated among the destination classes in proportion to each class's share of the total loss area, 40 stable controls (20 *Sasa* and 20 dwarf pine in both years), and 10 reverse transitions (dwarf pine→*Sasa*). Paired image crops from 2012 and 2021 were presented in random order with transition types concealed, and the interpreter was unaware that stable controls and reverse transitions were interleaved among the loss cells. Each sample included two pairs, one from the green-leaf season and the other from the autumn-color season. Frames with similar image greenness were paired to reduce misinterpretation arising from differences in leaf color between acquisition dates. The first author assigned each sample to one of the four interpretation categories: *Sasa* loss, canopy cover, boundary ambiguity, or indeterminate (full design and results in Table S5).

## Snowmelt pattern and trends {#sec-snowmelt}

For every 1 m cell, we compiled the annual snowmelt DOYs for 2011–2021 (10 observations per cell; 2019 is missing) and calculated (i) the **mean snowmelt date**, defined as the mean of these annual DOYs, which averages over interannual variation to represent the prevailing snowmelt timing at each location, and (ii) a **per-cell trend**, defined as the slope of an ordinary least-squares regression of annual DOY against year, estimated for cells with snowmelt detected in at least eight years. The trends were calculated for one purpose: to parameterize the snowmelt scenarios of the 2030 projections (@sec-projection). Per-cell slopes were tested with two-sided t-tests, with p-values adjusted across cells using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. To summarize change over the entire slope, we also averaged snowmelt DOY over all cells within each year and regressed these 10 annual spatial means on year; the slope of this regression is referred to as the **landscape trend**. As a perennial plant, *Sasa* is expected to respond to the prevailing local snowmelt timing rather than to snowmelt in any single year. Therefore, both models used the mean snowmelt date as an environmental predictor. Per-cell trends were not included as predictors because trend estimates are dominated by noise (see below) and adding the trend to Model B did not improve prediction in the held-out blocks (Table S1, Figure S4).

Given a 10-year record and a residual annual standard deviation (SD) of approximately nine days, the minimum detectable per-cell trend is approximately 2 days/year; therefore, trends of plausible magnitude cannot be detected reliably with this record. Accordingly, trends were used only to parameterize scenarios (@sec-projection), not as evidence of temporal change in snowmelt timing. Forecasting snowmelt timing itself was beyond the scope of this study.

## Statistical models {#sec-models}

The two questions outlined in the Introduction — whether expansion is associated mainly with environmental conditions or limited by distance from existing patches, and where establishment is expected next — were addressed using two models with a shared evaluation design.

**Shared predictors.** Both models used slope, elevation, topographic position index (TPI; the difference between the elevation of a cell and the mean elevation of its eight neighbors, distinguishing ridges from hollows), topographic wetness index (TWI; ln(a/tan β), with contributing area a and slope β [@Beven1979TWI]), northness (cos aspect), and eastness (sin aspect), together with the mean snowmelt date (@sec-snowmelt), as predictors. Terrain variables were derived from the Fundamental Geospatial Data DEM of the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan [@GSIdem] (approximately 5 m mesh) and reprojected to the analysis grid. Slope, aspect, and TPI were computed using the GDAL `gdaldem` utility, with slope and aspect calculated using the Zevenbergen–Thorne algorithm [@Zevenbergen1987ESPL]; TWI was computed in QGIS with SAGA GIS [@Conrad2015SAGA]. Therefore, the effective resolution of the terrain predictors was that of the source DEM rather than the 1 m analysis grid. Details of the terrain-variable derivation are provided in the Supporting Information. Because aspect is a circular variable, it was decomposed into northness and eastness before reprojection. Terrain roughness and terrain ruggedness index were excluded before modeling because of strong collinearity with slope (Spearman |r| = 0.93–0.97). All retained predictors had variance inflation factors of ≤2.30 and pairwise |r| of <0.7 (Table S7).

**Shared evaluation design.** Because neighboring cells are strongly spatially autocorrelated, cross-validation based on randomly sampled cells can overestimate predictive performance. Therefore, both models were evaluated using spatial blocks. The rectangular region enclosing all mapped cells (the analysis extent) was divided into a 10 × 10 grid of rectangular blocks (each approximately 180 × 175 m) using `spatialsample` [@spatialsample], and the blocks were randomly assigned to four groups (folds). Cells in a **held-out** fold were excluded from model fitting and used only for evaluation. The same blocks and folds were used for tuning, ensemble construction, and evaluation of both models, ensuring that model comparisons were based on identical held-out cells.

### Model A: environmental potential

Model A was a habitat suitability model fitted to the 2021 *Sasa* distribution. Presences were *Sasa* cells at 1 m resolution. Because the vegetation maps census the whole slope, non-*Sasa* cells are observed absences rather than pseudo-absences; absence cells were thinned to one per 5 m cell to reduce class imbalance, as *Sasa* occupies <1% of the classified area. Four algorithms were tuned in `tidysdm` [@tidysdm] using grid search with up to 18 candidates per algorithm: gradient-boosted trees [@Friedman2001GBM], MaxEnt [@Philips2006MaxEnt], random forest [@Breiman2001RandForest], and generalized additive models. Candidates were selected by TSS on spatial blocks and blended using LASSO-regularized stacking [@RCranStack]. The final ensemble composition is reported in the Results. Performance was reported as the True Skill Statistic (TSS; @Allouche2006TSS) and the area under the curve (AUC) on held-out spatial blocks. The main outputs were a continuous map of habitat suitability on a 0–1 scale (the suitability surface) and partial dependence profiles for each predictor, computed using the `DALEX` and `DALEXtra` packages. Where binarization was needed, we used the threshold maximizing TSS on predictions for held-out folds; the sensitivity of suitable area to thresholds of 0.1–0.7 is reported in Table S8. The main model used the full elevational range of the mapped slope. The results for a sensitivity variant restricting the domain to elevations below 2,560 m, which is the upper limit of the observed distribution, are provided in Table S6.

### Model B: establishment model

Model B directly modeled the observed establishment. For all cells that were non-*Sasa* in 2012 (n = 1,197,536), the response was whether they had become *Sasa* by 2021 (hereafter **establishment**; n = 4,095). This count includes 5,147 cells that were unclassified in 2012, none of which became *Sasa* (Table S3 is restricted to cells classified in both years). These non-*Sasa* 2012 cells, the only cells in which establishment could occur, are hereafter referred to as **eligible cells**. Predictors comprised the shared environmental predictors and distance from the 2012 *Sasa* front. Distance was calculated as the Euclidean distance to the nearest cell belonging to a 2012 *Sasa* patch exceeding 5 m² in geodesic area, with patches defined by 4-neighbor connectivity. This patch-size rule prevented tiny patches arising from classification noise from dominating the estimated expansion process: because area gain through rhizome elongation is proportional to patch perimeter, tiny patches with the highest perimeter-to-area ratios have disproportionate influence.

A binomial generalized additive model (GAM; `bam` in `mgcv` [@mgcvWood]) was fitted to all eligible cells, using thin-plate spline smooths for all predictors. The distance term used a logarithmic transformation, `s(log(1 + d))`, concentrating smooth flexibility near the front, where observations were densest (the criteria for the specification choice are provided in Table S9). The basis dimensions were k = 5 for the distance smooth and k = 10 for the environmental smooths. Model B was evaluated by leave-one-fold-out refitting on the shared blocks and folds (@sec-models): for each fold in turn, the model was refitted without that fold's cells and evaluated on them. As a robustness comparison, a gradient-boosted tree ensemble was also fitted to the same response and predictors on the same folds, using all establishment cells and a fold-stratified random sample of 150,000 non-establishment cells; because its negative set differs, its AUC is an approximate comparison. The estimated dispersal kernel was presented as the mean predicted establishment probability alongside the observed establishment rates in distance bands of 0–5, 5–10, 10–20, 20–40, 40–80, 80–160, and ≥160 m.

## Projections to 2030 {#sec-projection}

Model A's suitability map describes where the environment permits *Sasa* but contains no information on whether rhizomes can reach a location, so applying it directly to the future would greatly overestimate the near-term establishment area. The two modes of expansion were therefore treated separately. Rhizome expansion, which is limited by distance from existing fronts, was projected with a stochastic cellular automaton that applied Model B annually; dispersal limitation enters this projection through Model B's distance term, re-evaluated every year as the simulated fronts advance. Establishment from seeds is not limited by this distance process but could not be modeled from the 2012–2021 record, in which no new isolated patches were confirmed; for this mode, we instead present Model A's suitable area as a separate stratum of environmental potential (@sec-risky). Thus, projections of rhizome expansion arose from the expansion process itself rather than from a suitability threshold.

Starting from the observed 2021 distribution, the following steps were repeated for each year from 2022 to 2030: (i) recalculate the distance surface from the current simulated distribution using the same 5 m² patch rule as in model fitting; (ii) evaluate the 9-year establishment probability $p_9$ from Model B for every unoccupied cell, that is, the probability that the cell becomes *Sasa* over a 9-year interval like the fitting period, and convert it to an annual probability, $p_1 = 1 - (1 - p_9)^{1/9}$; and (iii) draw establishment independently for each cell from a Bernoulli distribution, retaining occupancy once established (assuming no loss within the 9-year period). For computational efficiency, the environmental component of the linear predictor was precomputed for each scenario × year, and only the distance term was updated within the simulation; this decomposition is exact (Supporting Information). We ran 200 replicates per scenario (50 for the spatial validation and structural sensitivity runs described below) and report per-cell establishment probabilities (means across replicates) and expected establishment area (the sum of probability × cell area); the latter requires no binarization threshold.

**Scenarios.** In the scenario with rate s (days/year), the mean snowmelt date of every cell was advanced by s × (year − 2016) days, where 2016 is the midpoint of the 2011–2021 averaging period; under s = −0.71 days/year, for example, snowmelt in 2030 occurs 9.9 days earlier than the 2011–2021 mean. In the main text, we report s = 0 (no change, consistent with the absence of a detectable trend) and s = −0.71 days/year (the mean of the per-cell slopes, close to the landscape trend of −0.69 days/year); s = −2.24 days/year (the lower 95% confidence limit of the landscape trend) is reported as an extreme scenario in Table S11. These are scenarios conditional on the observed decade, not forecasts of snowmelt. The shifts were spatially uniform because per-cell trend estimates are dominated by noise and cannot be directly extrapolated (@sec-snowmelt). The uniform shift is an approximation, justified in the Supporting Information, along with an assessment of the spatial structure of per-cell trends (Figure S4).

**Validation.** Three checks were conducted. (1) *Hindcast*: we tested whether simulations initialized from the 2012 distribution reproduced the observed 2012–2021 gross expansion. Because Model B was fitted to the same interval, this is a calibration check rather than an independent validation. (2) *Independent spatial validation*: for each spatial block, Model B was refitted excluding that block, and the hindcast was scored only within the omitted block. (3) *Structural sensitivity*: changes in the projections were quantified when the 5 m² patch rule was removed from distance updates, when annualization was replaced by the first-order approximation $p_9/9$, and when the no-loss assumption was relaxed by removing occupied cells each year with the annual probability implied by the observed 2012–2021 gross loss (29% over 9 years; 3.7%/year), with the distance surface recomputed after each year's losses.

## Risk to alpine communities {#sec-risky}

Two risk strata corresponding to the two modes of *Sasa* expansion are presented. The **rhizome stratum** comprised cellular-automaton establishment probabilities restricted to cells classified as other vegetation in 2021, a class dominated by alpine herbs and including snowbed communities of conservation concern, summarized as expected establishment area. To identify the communities at risk, we overlaid the 1:25,000 vegetation GIS map compiled under the National Survey on the Natural Environment by the Biodiversity Center of Japan, Nature Conservation Bureau, Ministry of the Environment (Hokuriku block) [@MOEvegmap2024] and cross-tabulated the expected establishment area by mapped community. The scale mismatch between the 1:25,000 polygons and the 1 m grid is addressed as a limitation in the Discussion. The **seed-dispersal stratum** represented environmental potential in 2021, namely cells at or above the TSS-maximizing threshold of Model A (Figure S7). Because establishment from seeds is not constrained by the modeled distance process, environmental potential provides a first approximation of the area that could be exposed; unmeasured factors, such as soils and constraints on seedling establishment, are not accounted for. Field validation of community composition and assessment of rare-species occurrence within risk areas remain future work.

## Software and reproducibility

All analyses used R 4.5.2 (terra, sf, tidymodels/tidysdm, stacks, spatialsample, mgcv, xgboost, ranger, maxnet, DALEX) in a scripted, non-interactive pipeline with fixed random seeds defined in a single configuration script; package versions are recorded in the `sessionInfo()` logs archived with the code. The vegetation classifier was implemented in Python using PyTorch, and image alignment used OpenCV. Code and data are archived at Zenodo (<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22745234>).
